claims.claim: Beautiful music in worship draws the heart to God.

stances.summary: Yes, the people are carried away by my hymns, and I do not deny it. Nothing has more power than a whole congregation singing its faith together.
stances.quote: They declare also that the people have been led astray by the strains of my hymns.  I certainly do not deny it. That is a lofty strain, and there is nothing more powerful than it.
stances.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H. T. F. Duckworth, NPNF second series vol. 10, 1896
stances.work: Sermon against Auxentius on the Giving Up of the Basilicas
stances.context: Preached at Milan in spring 386, when the Arian court tried to seize a church and his people kept watch inside it, singing. His opponents said he had bewitched the people with hymns; he accepts the charge. The power he names is the sung confession of the faith: the next sentence reads "For what has more power than the confession of the Trinity which is daily celebrated by the mouth of the whole people?" Augustine, Confessions 9.7.15, records that hymns and psalms were introduced at Milan at this very time, "after the manner of the Eastern Church", and in 9.6.14 that he wept at them. Several of Ambrose's own hymns survive (Augustine quotes Deus creator omnium). Orthodox; Doctor of the Church.

stances.summary: We are hard to draw to goodness, so the Holy Spirit mixed the sweetness of melody into His teaching. It works like a doctor who puts honey on the rim of a bitter cup.
stances.quote: He combined the delight of melody with His teaching, to the end that by the sweetness and softness of what we heard we might, all unawares, imbibe the blessing of the words.  He acted like wise leeches, who, when they would give sour draughts to sickly patients, put honey round about the cup.
stances.translation: Blomfield Jackson, NPNF second series vol. 8, 1895 (extract translated in his Prolegomena)
stances.location: section 1 (PG 29:212); English in the Prolegomena to NPNF second series vol. 8
stances.context: The honey is for "those who are boys in years, or at least but lads in ways of life", and the same passage adds a guard: we are to seek the things above "and not to allow ourselves to be degraded by our pleasure in the music to the lusts of the flesh." So melody is a means to the words, not the goal. In Letter 207 (c. 375, NPNF2 vol. 8) he defends the night psalmody of his churches against clergy of Neocaesarea, who objected to "psalms and a kind of music varying from the custom which has obtained among you"; he says the antiphonal singing gives "a heedful temper and a heart free from distraction". Orthodox.

stances.summary: Nothing lifts the soul toward God like a sacred song. God saw that we find holy reading hard, so He mixed melody into it, and now all sing His praise gladly.
stances.quote: For nothing, nothing so raises up the soul, gives it wings, sets it free from the earth, looses it from the chains of the body, makes it love wisdom and laugh at all the things of this life, as a harmonious melody and a divine song set in rhythm.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek (Migne, PG 55:156)
stances.original: Οὐδὲν γὰρ, οὐδὲν οὕτως ἀνίστησι ψυχὴν, καὶ πτεροῖ, καὶ τῆς γῆς ἀπαλλάττει, καὶ τῶν τοῦ σώματος ἀπολύει δεσμῶν, καὶ φιλοσοφεῖν ποιεῖ, καὶ πάντων καταγελᾷν τῶν βιωτικῶν, ὡς μέλος συμφωνίας, καὶ ῥυθμῷ συγκείμενον θεῖον ᾆσμα.
stances.work: Exposition of Psalm 41 (Psalm 42 in English Bibles)
stances.context: Just before, he says God, seeing many people sluggish and finding spiritual reading a labour, "mixed melody with prophecy" so that all, charmed by the rhythm, would send up the sacred hymns with eagerness. He goes on to set the psalms against the licentious songs of the theatre, and to insist on singing "in your hearts", with understanding, so that the mouth does not sing while the mind wanders. The same balance in Homily 9 on Colossians (John A. Broadus, NPNF1 vol. 13, 1889): Paul led people to psalms "that you might at once delight your soul with singing, and gently beguile your labors", and "Singing in your hearts to God. Not simply with the mouth, he means, but with heedfulness." The English printed on the catholiclibrary.org page is a modern rendering and was not used. Preached at Antioch, before 398. Orthodox.

stances.summary: God made the psalms a medicine that tastes sweet because it is sung. A psalm slips into the soul while it delights, and it stays in the memory.
stances.quote: For a psalm is heard with sweetness while it is sung. It gets into the soul while it delights. It is easily kept in mind when it is sung often.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin (A. E. Burn, Niceta of Remesiana, Cambridge 1905)
stances.original: Suauiter enim psalmus auditur dum canitur. Penetrat animum dum delectat. Facile retinetur dum frequentius psallitur.
stances.work: On the Good of Psalmody (De psalmodiae bono, also called De utilitate hymnorum)
stances.context: Bishop of Remesiana in Dacia (in modern Serbia), a friend of Paulinus of Nola, died after 414; not in the candidate pool. The sentence before says the Lord made through David a potion "sweet to the taste through song and strong to heal the wounds of sin" (the OCR reads "cafitionem" for "cantionem"). Chapter 2 answers people "not only in our parts but also in the East" who thought singing psalms and hymns superfluous and unfitting, since it is enough to sing in the heart; he praises those who sing with the voice too. Chapter 13 sets limits: the melody should suit holy religion, not "smell of the theatre", and should bring compunction for sin. Chapter 14 (in two manuscripts) says those who sing well "have a certain grace which stirs the hearers' minds to devotion", quoting Cyprian's letter to Donatus. The only English (Walsh, Fathers of the Church, 1949) is copyrighted. Orthodox.

stances.summary: People were charmed by heretical songs, so Ephrem set true teaching to the same tunes. His hymns gave the hearers delight and healing at once.
stances.quote: Ephraim adopted the music of the songs, but set them to piety, and so gave the hearers at once great delight and a healing medicine.
stances.translation: Blomfield Jackson, NPNF second series vol. 3, 1892
stances.context: This is a later historian's record of what Ephrem did (Theodoret wrote about 449; Ephrem died 373), not Ephrem's own words. Sozomen, Ecclesiastical History 3.16 (Hartranft, NPNF2 vol. 2, 1890), tells the same story: "When Ephraim perceived that the Syrians were charmed with the elegance of the diction and the rhythm of the melody" of Harmonius, son of Bardaisan, he wrote poems in the same metres "in accordance with the doctrines of the Church". Ephrem's own works are nearly all sung poems. In his own voice he calls himself God's harp ("Blessed be He Who has made me His harp!", Nisibene Hymn 17.12, Stopford, NPNF2 vol. 13, 1898) and says heretics "concealed the spikes amid melodies that they might not be perceived" (The Pearl, Hymn 5.5, J. B. Morris, NPNF2 vol. 13). The story that he trained choirs of women comes from Jacob of Serugh's verse homily on Ephrem (early 6th century), which exists in English only in a modern copyrighted translation; not checked here. Orthodox; Doctor of the Church.

stances.summary: Let a sober meal ring with psalms. If you have a good voice, use it: holy music that charms the ear is the best gift to your friends.
stances.quote: Let the temperate meal resound with psalms;  and as your memory is tenacious and your voice musical, undertake this office, as is your wont. You will provide a better entertainment for your dearest friends, if, while we have something spiritual to listen to, the sweetness of religious music charm our ears.
stances.context: Written about 246, soon after his conversion and before he became bishop. The setting is a meal among Christian friends, not the liturgy, so it shows his taste for sung devotion rather than a teaching about church music. About 400, Niceta of Remesiana (On the Good of Psalmody 14) quotes this passage to prove that good singers stir their hearers to devotion. Orthodox; martyred 258.

stances.summary: Let outsiders hear the church at prayer and the ringing sound of its hymns. Joyful sung praise pleases God and puts the devil to flight.
stances.quote: Let anyone standing outside the church hear the voice of the people at prayer; let him take note of the ringing sound of the hymns, and among the rites of the divine sacraments let him hear the answer of devout confession.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin (A. Zingerle, CSEL 22, 1891)
stances.original: audiat orantis populi consistens quis extra ecclesiam uocem, spectet celebres hymnorum sonitus et inter diuinorum quoque sacramentorum officia responsionem deuotae confessionis accipiat.
stances.location: on Psalm 65 (Psalm 66 in English Bibles), section 4
stances.context: The text at this url is a badly garbled OCR of the printed edition; the Latin given here is my cleaned reading of it (the OCR has, for example, "celehres hym- iioruni soiiitus"), so a machine check against the raw OCR will fail. Check the page scan on archive.org. He goes on to say that such exultant singing terrifies every adversary, wars against the devil, and is pleasing to God. On Psalm 64 (65), section 12, he calls "the delights of the morning and evening hymns" of the Church the greatest sign of God's mercy. Jerome (Lives of Illustrious Men 100) says Hilary wrote a book of hymns. Orthodox; Doctor of the Church.

stances.summary: The Psalms sweeten a hard road of virtue for beginners by setting it to melody, as doctors sweeten medicine with honey. But the melody points past itself, to a soul and a life in tune with God.
stances.quote: sweetened by something that delights the senses, as doctors are used to doing when they make some bitter, hard-to-swallow remedy easy for the sick to take by seasoning it with the pleasure of honey.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek (Gregorii Nysseni Opera vol. 5, p. 29)
stances.original: διά τινος τῶν τὴν αἴσθησιν εὐφραινόντων ἐφηδυνό μενα, καθάπερ καὶ τοῖς ἰατροῖς ποιεῖν σύνηθες, ὅταν τι πικρόν τε καὶ δύσληπτον τῶν ἀλεξητηρίων φαρμάκων 5.29 εὔληπτον ποιῶσι τοῖς ἀρρωστοῦσι τῇ τοῦ μέλιτος ἡδονῇ παραρτύοντες.
stances.work: On the Inscriptions of the Psalms
stances.location: part 1, end of chapter 2 (GNO 5:29); developed in chapter 3
stances.context: The subject of the sentence is the teaching of virtue, offered to "those who have not yet tasted the pure and divine pleasure". The same honey image as his brother Basil. Chapter 3 asks why David poured "this unspeakable and divine pleasure" over the teaching. He grants that singing the words is why we go through them with pleasure, then says there is something greater: the melody is an image of the harmony of all creation, which the mind hears "rising above the senses of the flesh", and a call to calm the passions. He adds that the Psalms' melodies are plain and unelaborate, unlike those of pagan composers. The page text keeps a line-break split ("ἐφηδυνό μενα") and the edition's page marker "5.29"; they are copied as they stand. English: Heine, 1995 (copyrighted). Orthodox.

stances.summary: Sing the psalms with understanding and a good rhythm, and they will quiet your passions. But psalmody is a step on the way; pure prayer is higher.
stances.quote: Pray gently and without agitation, and sing psalms with understanding and good rhythm, and you will be like a young eagle carried up on high. Psalmody lays the passions to rest and makes the body's lack of self-control grow still; prayer readies the mind to do its own proper work.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek (Migne, PG 79:1185, printed under the name of Nilus)
stances.original: Προσεύχου ἐπιεικῶς, καὶ ἀταράχως, καὶ ψάλλε συνετῶς καὶ εὐρύθμως, καὶ ἔσῃ ὡς νεοσσὸς ἀετοῦ ἐν ὕψει αἰρόμενος. ΚΕΦΑΛ. ΠΓʹ. Ἡ μὲν ψαλμῳδία τὰ πάθη κατευνάζει, καὶ τὴν ἀκρασίαν τοῦ σώματος ἠρεμεῖν ἀπεργάζεται. Ἡ δὲ προσευχὴ ἐνεργεῖν παρασκευάζει τὸν νοῦν τὴν ἰδίαν ἐνέργειαν.
stances.context: On Prayer came down under the name of Nilus of Ancyra, which is how Migne prints it; it is now accepted as the work of Evagrius. The chapter heading between the two sentences ("ΚΕΦΑΛ. ΠΓʹ.") is kept in the original as it stands on the page. Chapter 85 ranks the two: psalmody is a type of the manifold wisdom, but prayer is the prelude to immaterial knowledge. HETERODOX: his teaching was condemned with Origenism at the Council of Constantinople in 553. English: Bamberger 1970 and the Philokalia (Palmer, Sherrard and Ware, 1979), both copyrighted.

stances.summary: Singing in church moved me to tears, and it can lift weaker souls to God, so I lean toward keeping it. But when the tune moves me more than the words, I have sinned.
stances.quote: Thus vacillate I between dangerous pleasure and tried soundness; being inclined rather (though I pronounce no irrevocable opinion upon the subject) to approve of the use of singing in the church, that so by the delights of the ear the weaker minds may be stimulated to a devotional frame.
stances.translation: J. G. Pilkington, NPNF first series vol. 1, 1887
stances.context: Written about 397-400, as a bishop. The next sentence: "Yet when it happens to me to be more moved by the singing than by what is sung, I confess myself to have sinned criminally, and then I would rather not have heard the singing." He recalls weeping at the hymns of Milan at his baptism in 387 (9.6.14: "How greatly did I weep in Your hymns and canticles, deeply moved by the voices of Your sweet-speaking Church!"). In 10.33.49 he grants that minds are "more devoutly and earnestly elevated into a flame of piety by the holy words themselves when they are thus sung". He admits that at times he wished every melody banished from church, and admired Athanasius, whose reader chanted "more like speaking than singing". Elsewhere he is plainly for singing: Letter 55.34 (c. 400, J. G. Cunningham, NPNF1 vol. 1) calls it "so useful for inducing a devotional frame of mind and inflaming the strength of love to God"; on Psalm 99 (100) he praises wordless jubilation, "a certain sound of joy without words". His doubt is about the pull of the sound over the sense, not about singing itself. Orthodox; Doctor of the Church.

stances.summary: The psalms are sung to put the soul in tune, not to please the ear. Singing well is good for the soul and helps those who hear, but singing for the pleasure of the sound misses the point.
stances.quote: Some simple people among us, though they believe the words are inspired by God, still think the psalms are sung to a tune for the sake of fine sound and to please the ear. It is not so. Scripture did not seek what is sweet and persuasive. This too was ordained for the good of the soul.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek (Migne, PG 27:37-40)
stances.original: Τινὲς µὲν γὰρ τῶν παρ' ἡµῖν ἀκεραίων, καί τοι πιστευόντων εἶναι θεόπνευστα τὰ ῥήµατα, ὅµως νοµίζουσι διὰ τὸ εὔφωνον καὶ τέρψεως ἕνεκεν τῆς ἀκοῆς µελῳδεῖσθαι τοὺς ψαλµούς. [00522] Οὐκ ἔστι δὲ οὕτως· [00523] οὐ γὰρ τὸ ἡδὺ καὶ πιθανὸν ἐζήτησεν ἡ Γραφή· [00524] ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῦτο ὠφελείας ἕνεκεν τῆς ψυχῆς τετύπωται
stances.work: Letter to Marcellinus on the Interpretation of the Psalms
stances.context: Sections 27-29 give his reasons for singing the psalms: God is to be praised with the full voice, and singing images and trains a soul whose reason, desire and anger move together in harmony, like a lyre under the plectrum. He does commend it: singing smooths what is rough in the soul and heals grief, and those who sing with the tongue and the mind together greatly help their hearers. Those who sing only for pleasure "please themselves" and deserve blame. Section 29 sums up: to say the psalms with melody is not a striving after fine sound but a sign of the harmony of the thoughts in the soul. Augustine (Confessions 10.33.50) had heard that Athanasius "obliged the reader of the psalm to give utterance to it with so slight an inflection of voice, that it was more like speaking than singing"; that is a report, not his own words. The PDF text uses the micro sign for mu, keeps line-break splits, and inserts the site's bracketed paragraph numbers; the original is copied as it stands. The only full English (a Religious of C.S.M.V., 1953) is copyrighted. Orthodox; Doctor of the Church.

stances.summary: Christians may sing, even to the lyre, but only sober and temperate music. Pipes, drums and sensuous tunes belong to drunken revels; the one instrument we truly use is the Word.
stances.quote: For temperate harmonies are to be admitted; but we are to banish as far as possible from our robust mind those liquid harmonies, which, through pernicious arts in the modulations of tones, train to effeminacy and scurrility.
stances.context: The chapter is about how Christians behave at banquets, not about the church service. He writes "The one instrument of peace, the Word alone by which we honour God, is what we employ", reads the instruments of Psalm 150 as the tongue, the mouth and the body, and banishes pipes and flutes as fit for beasts; yet he allows "even if you wish to sing and play to the harp or lyre, there is no blame", and calls the psalm "a melodious and sober blessing". Chromatic harmonies are left "to immodest revels". Written at Alexandria about 190-200. Venerated in the early church; dropped from the Roman Martyrology in the 16th century, but never condemned.

stances.summary: Choosing ministers for their lovely voices is a bad custom. While a sweet voice is sought, a holy life is neglected, and the singer delights the people while he provokes God.
stances.quote: So it often happens that, while a pleasing voice is sought for the sacred ministry, no one troubles to seek a fitting life, and the singing minister provokes God by his conduct while he delights the people with his voice.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin (MGH Epistolae I, p. 363)
stances.original: Unde fit plerumque, ut ad sacrum ministerium, dum blanda vox quaeritur, quaeri congrua vita neglegatur et cantor minister Deum moribus stimulet, cum populum vocibus delectat.
stances.work: Decree of the Roman synod of July 595 (Register of Letters)
stances.context: The Latin was read as quoted in full from the MGH edition in footnote 8 of Franck Quoëx's article at this url; I could not load the edition, and the NPNF selection does not translate this decree. The decree ends the Roman custom of deacons singing the psalms at Mass: deacons are to be free for preaching and almsgiving, and subdeacons or minor clergy are to sing. On the other side, Homilies on Ezekiel 1.1.15 (593) says that the voice of psalmody, when done with the intent of the heart, prepares a way for the Almighty into the heart, so that He pours into the attentive mind the mysteries of prophecy or the grace of compunction. I saw that line only as quoted by Aquinas (Commentary on the Psalms, prologue) and Hugh of Fouilloy, not in an edition of Gregory. So: singing with the heart, yes; valuing the voice, no. Orthodox; Doctor of the Church.

stances.summary: Theatrical singing in church, especially by women, stirs up desire instead of repentance.
stances.quote: Isidore of Pelusium also complained of the theatrical singing, especially that of the women, which, instead of inducing penitence for sin, tended much more to awaken sinful desires
stances.translation: McClintock and Strong, Cyclopaedia of Biblical, Theological, and Ecclesiastical Literature (1867-1887), article "Music, Christian" (a summary, not his words)
stances.work: Letters (as summarised by a secondary source)
stances.location: the source cites only "Biblioth. Patr. 7:543"; usually given as Letter 1.90
stances.context: A monk and priest near Pelusium in Egypt, died about 450; not in the candidate pool. I could not load the Greek (PG 78) or any public-domain English of the letter, so this rests on a 19th-century summary and is unverified. His objection, as summarised, is to theatrical and sensual singing, not to psalmody as such.

stances.summary: Sing to God with the heart, not with the voice. Church is not a theatre, and a man with a poor voice but good works is a sweet singer to God.
stances.quote: Let the young men hear this; let those whose office is to sing psalms in church hear it: we must sing to God not with the voice but with the heart. Throat and jaws are not to be smeared with sweet medicine, as tragic actors do, so that theatre tunes and songs are heard in church. We sing in fear, in works, in knowledge of the Scriptures.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin (Migne, PL 26:528-529)
stances.original: Audiant haec adolescentuli: audiant hi quibus psallendi in ecclesia officium est, Deo non voce, sed corde cantandum: nec in tragoedorum modum guttur et fauces dulci medicamine colliniendas, ut in ecclesia theatrales moduli audiantur et cantica, sed in timore, in opere, in scientia Scripturarum.
stances.context: Written at Bethlehem about 386-388. He goes on: "Even if someone is, as they call it, bad-voiced, if he has good works he is a sweet singer before God. Let the servant of Christ so sing that not the voice of the singer but the words that are read give pleasure", so that the evil spirit that troubled Saul is driven out, not brought into those "who have made a stage of God's house". He is not against singing as such; just before, he says we ought to sing and praise the Lord "more with the mind than with the voice". His target is vocal display and the sweetness of the voice. The same Latin stands in Gratian's Decretum, Distinction 92, chapter 1 (https://geschichte.digitale-sammlungen.de/decretum-gratiani/kapitel/dc_chapter_0_980). The page at the url is a database of sources quoted in organ sermons; it reproduces Migne's text. Orthodox; Doctor of the Church.

splits_fathers: Almost every early Christian who wrote on it held that singing psalms and hymns in worship is good and moves the soul toward God: Ambrose, Basil, Chrysostom, Niceta, Ephrem, Hilary, Cyprian, Gregory of Nyssa and Evagrius all say so, several emphatically. Nearly all add a guard: the words, the heart and the life matter more than the sound, theatrical or sensual music is out, and instruments are not used in church. The real division is over beauty itself. Basil, Chrysostom, Niceta and Ambrose treat the sweetness of melody as God's own device for drawing people. Athanasius, Jerome and Gregory the Great say the pleasure of the sound is not the point and can be a danger. Augustine is torn between the two and says so. The only voices against singing as such are anonymous and reported in order to be answered: people "in our parts and in the East" who thought singing superfluous (Niceta, On the Good of Psalmody 2; his editor Burn suggests the Council of Laodicea's limits on congregational singing lie behind it), and the clergy of Neocaesarea who objected to Basil's new psalmody (Letter 207). So there are real named voices on both sides, but only if the statement is about beauty (sound, voice, melody), not about singing in worship. Named voices who flatly disagree are few: Jerome is the clearest.
splits_people_today: Most churchgoers would agree: music is central to evangelical, Catholic and Orthodox worship, and many people outside church say music is where they feel closest to something beyond themselves. A real minority would disagree or hesitate: people who distrust emotional or concert-style worship, those in a cappella and plain-psalm traditions (Churches of Christ, some Reformed and Anabaptist churches), Quakers who worship in silence, and anyone who thinks feelings stirred by music are easily mistaken for faith. Non-religious people would often grant that music produces spiritual feeling but reject "draws the heart to God". As worded, the claim is lopsided toward agree. A sharper wording splits people better and matches the real patristic divide, for example "A beautiful voice or tune matters in worship" against "Plain singing is best; beauty can distract", or Augustine's worry, "I am sometimes moved more by the music than by the words".

misattributions.truth: Not found in Augustine's works. The nearest real line is usually given as Expositions of the Psalms, on Psalm 72 (73), section 1: "qui enim cantat laudem, non solum laudat, sed etiam hilariter laudat" (whoever sings praise not only praises but praises joyfully). The NPNF translation on newadvent.org abridges that section and omits the sentence; the Latin was not checked here.

misattributions.line: Woe to us, my son, the days are coming when monks will forsake the solid food of the Holy Spirit and turn to songs and tunes (Pambo warning a disciple who had learned troparia and canons in Alexandria).
misattributions.truth: Apocryphal. It is not in the Sayings of the Desert Fathers; it names "canons", a hymn form of the 7th-8th centuries, and scholars (for example James McKinnon) date the story to the 6th century at the earliest. It was printed by Gerbert in 1784 and is repeated as 4th-century in older reference works such as McClintock and Strong.

misattributions.line: Instruments suit children; they were removed from the churches and plain singing was kept.
misattributions.truth: From the Questions and Answers to the Orthodox (question 107), a 5th-century work printed among Justin's writings and now usually assigned to Theodoret of Cyrrhus or his circle. Not checked in the source here.

misattributions.line: Gregorian chant was composed or collected by Pope Gregory the Great.
misattributions.truth: A legend first told in the 9th century (John the Deacon's Life of Gregory, about 873). The chant repertoire that bears his name took shape in the 8th-9th centuries, and no writing of Gregory mentions composing or collecting chant; his one recorded ruling on church singing (the synod of 595) restricts who sings.

misattributions.line: Not like the comedians should they raise their sweet and liquid notes to entertain the assembly with theatrical songs and melodies in the church...
misattributions.truth: A loose 19th-century English paraphrase (McClintock and Strong) of Jerome's Commentary on Ephesians 5:19, with sentences Jerome did not write. Use the Latin (PL 26:528-529) or a close rendering of it.

notes: Best pair for the reveal: Basil's honey on the rim of the cup (the sweetness of melody is God's gift for drawing us) against Jerome's "not with the voice but with the heart", with Augustine's tears and fears in the middle. Chrysostom's line on Psalm 41 is the most vivid "agree" but is my own rendering from Greek; Ambrose, Basil, Augustine, Clement, Cyprian and Theodoret-on-Ephrem are public-domain English copied from the page. Neutral on beauty, useful only if a statement is about attention rather than sound: Benedict, Rule 19, "sic stemus ad psallendum, ut mens nostra concordet voci nostrae" (let us so stand to sing that our mind is in harmony with our voice; Latin at thelatinlibrary.com/benedict.html), and Rule 47 (only those who can sing so that the hearers are edified should do so, not checked here); Cassian, Institutes 2.11 (NPNF2 vol. 11), where the Egyptian monks "consider it better for ten verses to be sung with understanding and thought than for a whole Psalm to be poured forth with a bewildered mind". Instruments are a separate question with a near-unanimous early answer (not in church) and a live split today (organ and band against a cappella). No recorded words on music were found for Macrina, Antony, Moses the Black, Arsenius, Poemen, Tertullian, Origen, Pelagius, Martin, Paulinus or Boethius in the time spent; this was not an exhaustive search. Boethius (On Music 1.1) holds that music shapes character for good or ill, but not about worship. Verification was kept light at the user's request: every PD English quote and every Greek or Latin original except Hilary's was copied from the fetched page text by script.
